One. The owner of himself always grieves and melts. We became…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

Saadi Pharmacy

One.
The owner of himself always grieves and melts.
We became the owner of a full-bodied kingdom and were freed.
(Saadi)
When we consider ourselves our own owner, we melt from grief. When we consider the kingdom and the owned to belong to that beautiful Unique One, we become free and liberated. "Inna lillah" means we belong to Him. We are not our own owners.

▫️Two.
Every foot that entered the house found a treasure;
No longer would all its life be at the market.
(Saadi)
There is a treasure that is found in the realm of the heart. One who finds the way to the inner treasure is freed from dependence on markets. Bayazid Bastami said about the meaning of dervishhood: "The one who, in the corner of his own heart, finds a foot entering a treasure..."

▫️Three.
One who became a stranger to wealth and greatness and lordship,
Is familiar to whomever he reaches.
(Saadi)
One who sees himself free from names and positions and passing powers can be familiar and close to everyone. If we are captivated by our own greatness and lordship and wealth, if we are bound by our position and name and reputation and intelligence and knowledge, we lose the felicity of "familiarity."

▫️Four.
Whoever does not know gratitude for today's blessing
Will eat regret upon the portion of tomorrow's mercy.
(Saadi)
One who does not appreciate the gifts of this world and does not welcome them with gratitude and joy will also be deprived of the mercy of the next world.

Whoever does not see today in the world the countenance of the Friend,
It is most likely that tomorrow he will have no vision.
(Saadi)
The beauty of nature and the movement and growth of the earth is a mercy of this world:
"Fa-unzur ila athar rahmatillah kayfa yuhyi al-arda ba'da mawtiha" (Surah Rum, verse 50)
"Look at these signs of Allah's kindness, how He revives the earth after its death." (Translation of Tafsir Kashf al-Asrar)

▫️Five.
Except the remembrance of the Friend, whatever you do is wasted life;
Except the secret of love, whatever you say is vanity.
(Saadi)
If life is not mixed with the remembrance of the Friend, and is not spent in longing for the Friend, it is wasted. It has passed in vanity:
Saadi, if he does not risk love, what shall he do with the kingdom of existence?
It is a pity that a whole life should go to waste.

The remembrance and recollection of the Friend has no end. It is not tiresome either. Because it is the food of the soul. The bread and water of the soul:
Our speech grew long and still remains,
For the remembrance of the Friend brings no weariness whatsoever.
(Saadi)
Therefore, his regret is for the times that passed unaware of the Friend:
Whatever we said other than the tale of the Friend,
In all our life we regret it.
(Saadi)
If there is any regret, it is nothing but this: why did we not breathe in His remembrance more? Why did we not throb in longing for Him more?
So that precious life does not end in regret,
All night Your remembrance was ongoing and repeated.

Speaking with Him, speaking of Him, and floating in the "tale of the Friend" is the meaning of life.

〰 Seddiq Qotbi

There was a time when economic sanctions were presented as an alternative to war, and many hoped this approach could resolve international disputes without war and destruction, while others dismissed it as ineffective. But as time passed, these assumptions were met with fundamental doubts. It gradually became clear that economic sanctions leave irreversible damage in people's lives.

Mohammad Javad Dashti-Manesh, an economic researcher, examines in this piece one of the studies conducted on the intergenerational effects of sanctions on the educational future of Iranian children, emphasizing that economic pressures must not be allowed to narrow children's educational opportunities and growth.

Israel, in violation of the UN Charter, has attacked the capitals of its neighbors, and numerous instances of violations of international humanitarian law have been documented regarding its actions, yet it maintains its nuclear arsenal without accepting similar restrictions. In contrast, Iran — which for two centuries has not waged any war except in self-defense — is targeted with sanctions and attacks, while its nuclear facilities remain under the safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Regarding the Strait of Hormuz, Pezeshkian said they have tried to close this strait to Iran, while they themselves have used the same route to transfer missiles and weapons to the region. The law of the sea considers such a situation illegal. The 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea — to some of whose rules Washington refers but which it has not itself ratified — stipulates that ships passing through an international strait must refrain from any threat or use of force against the coastal states of that strait. Under the rule of innocent passage as well, a ship whose passage serves an attack on a coastal state no longer qualifies as "innocent passage." Iran will not accept being deprived of its territorial waters while others use those same waters to transfer instruments of war against it.

Pezeshkian concluded by emphasizing the indivisibility of security: security either exists for all countries of the region or for no one. This idea has a long history. European states included it in 1975 in the Helsinki Final Act and reaffirmed it in 1999, committing themselves not to strengthen their own security at the expense of reducing the security of others.

Pezeshkian said: "We want strong neighbors." He emphasized that Iran has always been ready for diplomacy, "without accepting the language of force."

God, keep us away from that patriotism that only shows up on days of victory. Teach us to love Iran not when it bends to our wishes, but precisely in the moment we are furious with it, complaining about its rulers, and seeing its future as bleak. God, protect us from the temptation of those saviors who must first set the land ablaze so they can build their promised tomorrow on its ashes. Do not let us become among those who sacrifice independence for the sake of freedom; the people for the sake of power; and Iran for the sake of proving themselves right. How easy it is to stand far away and write prescriptions of courage for a people who must pay the price. How easy it is to call for war when it is someone else's child who must die in it. How easy it is to call destruction a "transition" when the house collapsing is not our own. God, deliver us from addiction to hatred; from that hatred that no longer seeks truth, no longer seeks a solution, and does not even seek victory; it only wants the other to be destroyed, even if the homeland itself is wounded in the process. Give us the maturity to tell the difference between opposition and revenge, between protest and destruction, between hope and delusion, and between saving a nation and seizing its future. God, do not let us one day grow so thirsty for power that we clasp the hand of any foreigner who promises tomorrow. Do not let us turn foreign policy from prudence in service of Iran's interests into a weapon of factional strife; today in the name of one group and tomorrow in the name of another, but always at the expense of the country that must remain above us all. Do not let us put national security on the table of personal gain; for a contract, for wealth, for a position, for a share of power, or to secure our own future, let us not make a people pay with their future who have no stake in our bargain. Do not let us grow so sick of today that we mistake any tomorrow for liberation, simply because it is different. Do not let us invoke the name of the people on our lips while in private thinking only of our own standing after the storm. If we speak, let it not be for a share in the tomorrow of power. If we oppose, let it not be to cut a deal with would-be victors. If we stand, let it not be in the ranks of this camp or that camp, but alongside a people who are always the first victims of the game of power. God, teach us that sometimes patriotism is not a shout, not a flag, not a slogan, but the ability to say a single "no": no to tyranny, no to disintegration, no to war, no to dependency, no to revenge, and no to a future that can only be built by destroying Iran today.

Each time, my answer was Ayatollah al-Uzma Shobeiry Zanjani. A first-rate jurist, and outstanding in rijal. But he combined this jurisprudential and scholarly standing with qualities that are rarer still. He, his household, and those around him lived with great integrity and an intense sensitivity to financial propriety. He was humble in a way seldom seen and indifferent to the conventional protocols of marja'iyat, and despite absolute jurisprudential authority, he made no effort whatsoever to attract devotees and followers or to acquire prestige, status, fame, or power. He was spiritual—a "man of God"—and his serenity, his piety, and his prayers were a sight to behold. He was one of those of whom it is said, in a saying attributed to Jesus Christ: "Whoever's sight reminds you of God, whose knowledge adds to your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desire goodness." In addition to his morning teaching, he held a gathering at his home an hour before maghrib, which in my view—if the hawza's "scholarly gathering" were ever to be registered as an "intangible heritage"—would be a perfect example; and for me, a mere outsider, every time I attended, its atmosphere and details were a spectacle to behold. He also possessed a cultivated aesthetic sensibility, evident in, among other things, his beautiful handwriting and his exceedingly delicate gaze and body language. He never sought perks, resources, or privileges, and he used his considerable spiritual influence over the system's high-ranking officials solely to unblock people's difficulties and help the oppressed. entry.summary:

The book "In Defense of Universal Basic Services" rests on three theoretical pillars: human needs, the capability approach, and foundational economics and provisioning systems. The authors argue that compared to Universal Basic Income (UBI), the idea of Universal Basic Services (UBS)—by rebuilding social infrastructure and collective consumption while also enhancing efficiency and ecological sustainability—strengthens equality and solidarity as well, and is politically feasible because it is incremental and adaptable in nature. But you could see that the sustained presence of part of society in the public space was effectively producing a different image of the street: the street was not entirely in the hands of a single force. And it is precisely at this point that internal simplification can also ruin the analysis. If, because of the radical slogans of the third group, we treat the entire gathering as a factional movement, we have conflated the first body with the third group. If, because of the presence of needy people next to the mokebs, we assume the whole crowd was "brought in with food," we have substituted a social situation for a political explanation. And in the opposite direction, if, because of the presence of families and their genuine emotions, we deny any formal organizing or factional activity on the margins of the gatherings, we have once again erased part of the scene. Perhaps the most important difference between a television report and field observation is this. The camera passes over the crowd and turns a thousand people into one "people." The politician speaks from behind a desk about those same thousand people and turns them into one "current." Social media clips a few seconds of the most radical slogan and turns a thousand people into those same few who shouted loudest. But when you walk among them yourself, this unity quickly comes apart. One has come to recite prayers. One has come to say that in wartime you don't stay home. One has come because it's night and the square is crowded. One stands next to the mokeb because life has become expensive. And one is waiting for the ceremony to end so he can just begin his own political work. If we look at the past hundred years, a large part of Iran's political history can perhaps be understood as the successive efforts of governments to build this same "state capacity" and, as a result, achieve practical independence. Reza Shah, above all else, advanced the project of territorial control: a centralized army, a bureaucracy, roads, registration, taxation, and extending the authority of the central government into regions where the state's presence had previously been weak or indirect. During Mohammad Reza Shah's era, and in a different and more overt form during the Mosaddegh movement, the question of economic independence and sovereignty over resources—especially oil—moved to the center of politics. The Islamic Republic pursued a different project: popularizing politics and mobilizing society, while simultaneously building a military and deterrent capacity unlike the classic Reza Shah-era army model. The recent war with America may be the clearest test of this transformation. Iran today, regardless of any judgment about its policies and the heavy costs of the war, is no longer the state whose official delegation needed the British to repair its car just to get through Qazvin. In today's war, against a power with overwhelming air, naval, intelligence, and economic superiority, it was able to keep fighting for months, respond to American bases with missiles and drones, and use geography, missiles, drones, regional networks, and the Strait of Hormuz to impose costs on America and its allies. The concept of independence must be sought not only in slogans and legal sovereignty, but in "the ability to resist the will of a greater power." Over the span of a hundred years, Iran's territory and core problem have not changed much: building a state that can control its territory, take command of its resources, organize its society, and—at the moment of external pressure—ensure its decisions are not independent merely on paper. The difference is that the tools of this capacity have today come to consist of a combination of social capacity, military technology, deterrence, and the power to impose costs.
